q: Does the bacteriocin-plasmid-carrying oral/skin-commensal S. epidermidis lineage (KSE56/KSE650 style, epidermin/nukacin producers) confer measurable colonization-resistance against S. aureus and MRSA in the human nasal/nares microbiome in vivo?
basis: Nakazono 2022 sequenced complete epidermin (pEpi56) and nukacin (pNuk650) plasmids from oral S. epidermidis and confirmed the gene clusters and peptide identities that would be required for anti-staphylococcal activity. Colonization-resistance against S. aureus/MRSA in vivo (as opposed to in-vitro inhibition on plates) is not addressed and is a separate question about ecological fitness in the anterior nares and skin, where S. epidermidis competes directly with S. aureus.
next_steps: Cross-sectional 16S/shotgun metagenomic screen of paired nares samples typing bacteriocin-plasmid carriage vs S. aureus/MRSA carriage state.
Prospective longitudinal cohort tracking whether bacteriocin-plasmid+ S. epidermidis colonization at baseline predicts reduced S. aureus/MRSA acquisition.
Controlled murine nasal-colonization competition assays with isogenic S. epidermidis pairs (plasmid-cured vs plasmid-bearing) challenged with S. aureus.

q: How stable are the epi and nuk gene clusters when carried on plasmids (as in pEpi56 / pNuk650) versus when integrated on the chromosome, and how readily do these plasmids horizontally transfer to other skin-community staphylococci (S. hominis, S. capitis, S. warneri)?
basis: Nakazono 2022 documents that these bacteriocin clusters are plasmid-borne in KSE56 and KSE650 and that pNuk650 shares a 99.6% backbone with the reference nukacin plasmid pIVK45 but carries a ~8 kbp insertion with additional ORFs. BV-BRC PlasmidFinder rep typing (this replication) places pNuk650 and pIVK45 in the same replicon lineage (repUS46, repUS23_repA/SAP099B, rep21/pWBG754) while pEpi56 has a divergent rep39/rep5a-like replicon. Plasmid stability under non-selective growth and inter-species conjugative/mobilizable transfer frequency were not measured.
next_steps: Serial-passage plasmid-retention assays (with and without bacteriocin-target selection) to quantify per-generation loss rate.
In-vitro filter-mating conjugation assays from KSE56/KSE650 into recipient S. hominis, S. capitis, S. warneri, and S. aureus strains, quantifying transfer frequency by replicon.

Comparative genomics of publicly available skin-commensal Staphylococcus genomes for the SAP099B / rep39 replicon lineages carrying epi/nuk cassettes, to see whether horizontal transfer has already left a signal in the wild.

q: Can bacteriocin-producing S. epidermidis strains of this class be rationally engineered or selected as a topical/intranasal probiotic for S. aureus / MRSA decolonization, and would such a product show clinically meaningful efficacy compared to mupirocin?
basis: Nakazono 2022 provides the sequence-verified genetic parts list (complete epi and nuk clusters, self-immunity genes, plasmid backbones) that would underpin such a probiotic strategy, and this replication confirmed the peptide identities (100% aa identity to canonical Tü3298 epidermin; identical mature nukacin C-terminal). Whether a defined probiotic strain built on these parts is safe, stably colonizing, and clinically effective for decolonization is not addressed.
next_steps: Preclinical safety and colonization-persistence testing of a candidate KSE56- or KSE650-derived strain in a human skin-microbiome model (ex-vivo skin explants, humanized mice).
Head-to-head in-vitro potency panels vs mupirocin, retapamulin, and lysostaphin against a diverse MRSA clinical isolate collection, including mupirocin-resistant lineages.
Design a phase 1/2 randomized decolonization trial (nasal + skin) in MRSA-colonized patients, with strain persistence and S. aureus load as co-primary endpoints.

q: Do the epi (epiE/F/G/H) and nuk (nukF/E/G/H) immunity-gene cassettes present on pEpi56 and pNuk650 provide the full self-protection observed for the producer strain, and how should bioinformatic bacteriocin-gene-cluster predictions be interpreted when the immunity cassette is partial or absent?
basis: This replication confirmed the complete presence of the annotated immunity-gene cassettes on both plasmids (epiE, epiF, epiG, epiH on pEpi56; nukF, nukE, nukG, nukH on pNuk650), but the paper measures functional self-immunity only implicitly (the strains are viable producers). The general question of what minimum immunity-gene set is required to prevent producer self-killing --- and therefore what bioinformatic bacteriocin predictions actually predict when immunity genes are missing --- is not resolved.
next_steps: Systematic single- and combinatorial-knockout of epiE/F/G/H and nukF/E/G/H in the native producer background, scoring self-viability and mature-bacteriocin secretion.
Heterologous expression of the biosynthesis cluster with and without each immunity subcluster in a naive Staphylococcus recipient, to isolate the immunity contribution.
Benchmark BAGEL4 / antiSMASH bacteriocin predictions against known immunity-complete vs immunity-partial reference plasmids, and publish a curated interpretation guideline.

q: Under sustained epidermin or nukacin selective pressure, what is the resistance-development trajectory in target S. aureus / MRSA populations, and does that resistance cross-confer to therapeutic lantibiotics such as nisin or mersacidin?
basis: Nakazono 2022 established the antibacterial activity of KSE56 and KSE650 supernatants at a phenotypic level and confirmed the complete biosynthetic capability from the plasmid sequences (this replication verified the sequence side). The kinetics and mechanism of S. aureus adaptation to epidermin/nukacin pressure --- and cross-resistance to clinically relevant lantibiotics --- are not addressed and are directly relevant to any probiotic or peptide-drug development path.
next_steps: Serial-passage evolution experiments with S. aureus / MRSA under sub-inhibitory epidermin and nukacin exposure, whole-genome sequencing of resistant isolates.
Cross-resistance panels of evolved resistant lineages against nisin, mersacidin, gallidermin, and lysostaphin.
Mechanistic follow-up on candidate resistance mutations (lipid II biosynthesis genes, cell-wall modification systems, dltABCD, mprF) using isogenic knock-in strains.
